entries.note: From Old French art and Latin [[from:ars]], also used for practical skills and crafts, from a root meaning to fit together; related to [[same-root:arma]].
Latin for weapons, related to [[same-root:art]] because using weapons takes skill.
Its art- comes from [[from:art]], the idea of creating something; originally not negative, compare Latin [[from:artificium]].
German for art, which gave German [[gave:künstlich]] for artificial, the same journey English took from [[equivalent:art]] to artifice.
German for [[equivalent:artificial]], formed from [[from:Kunst]], art.
The German term for AI, built on [[from:künstlich]], which Rob finds cool because it links back to the word for art.
Latin for a work of art, a skill, a theory or a system, showing [[see:artificial]] was not originally negative.
Something fashioned with skill.
Entered English from French in the 14th century, literally meaning made of hemp, so related to [[same-root:cannabis]]; became popular with painters because Venice had plenty.
Related to [[same-root:canvas]], a cloth made of hemp.
A particularly tightly woven canvas; its duck comes from a Dutch word, and it gave its name to [[gave:duct tape]].
Originally duck tape, non-adhesive strips of [[from:cotton duck]]; the name passed to adhesive tape in World War II, and duct is a folk etymology.
Canvassing opinion is the same word as [[same-root:canvas]], evoking gathering opinions in a cloth bag; spelled with two S's to tell them apart.
A white preparatory coating, borrowed from Italian for chalk or plaster, from Latin [[from:gypsum]]; originally rabbit-skin glue with chalk, used on wooden panels from the 13th century.
Called the Greek although Venetian, raised in Crete under Venetian rule and working in Italy and Spain; the name suits a foreigner who signed in Greek script.
From the Dutch for donkey, something that carries things, like a [[see:clothes horse]]; so a canvas on an easel is a donkey carrying marijuana.
Compared with [[see:easel]]: both name a carrying animal for something that holds things.
From Dutch [[from:schets]], from Italian [[from:schizzo]], ultimately from Greek [[from:skhedios]], something temporary or offhand.
From Dutch [[from:etsen]], to cause to be eaten, so related to [[same-root:eat]]; etching eats away at a surface; unrelated to [[unrelated:sketch]] despite both being Dutch.
Related to [[same-root:etch]].
Dutch for landship, introduced as landskip by Henry Peacham in 1607; calling a real view a landscape figuratively invokes a painting.
The suffix of friendship and championship, matching the Dutch ending of [[see:landscape]].
Taking a chunk of a word and applying it elsewhere, usually the wrong chunk; maybe what happened with -scape in [[see:seascape]].
Formed by taking -scape from [[from:landscape]], not borrowed directly from Dutch.
Another word using the -scape taken from [[from:landscape]].
17th-century boom in Dutch painting, funded by trade wealth and a middle class buying art, explaining English's Dutch art words.
Known by his first name; his full name Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn includes the patronymic son of Harmen and of the river Rhine.
Strictly he should be called Leonardo, since da Vinci only means of Vinci.
His first name was Michelangelo, a name already taken; known for dramatic lighting, [[see:tenebrism]].
Full name Pablo Ruiz Picasso; he went by his mother's surname rather than his father's, and is known by one name like older masters.
Called by his surname though people know he was Salvador, like [[see:Picasso]].
Rob tries the Dutch pronunciation and wonders whether a name meaning from Gogh suits him, suggesting just Vincent.
1600–1750 style of drama and grandeur; French for irregular or bizarre, probably from Portuguese for an irregular pearl, applied pejoratively by later critics; related to [[same-root:verruca]].
Dramatic lighting in which figures emerge from deep darkness, favoured by [[see:Caravaggio]].
The artistic use of strong contrasts between dark and light to create volume and depth.
Shares a Latin root beginning with V with [[same-root:Baroque]], the idea being something warty, lumpy and irregular.
A lighter late [[see:Baroque]]; means shell or rock work, from French [[from:rocaille]], playfully altered; critics used it for anything frivolous or excessively ornate.
Named by critics who disliked it, probably after Monet's [[from:Impression, soleil levant]]; it conveys an impression of a scene with visible brushstrokes.
Came before [[see:impressionism]], apparently coined in [[see:Louis Leroy]]'s scathing 1874 review of paintings including Monet's.
The murky [[see:Claude Monet]] painting whose title probably gave [[gave:impressionism]] its name.
Impressionist whose paintings were targeted in the review that coined [[see:impressionist]].
Critic whose 1874 review used [[see:impressionist]], praising only the bread, grapes and chair in Monet's Breakfast.
A reaction to [[see:impressionism]], expressing inner experience through distorted forms and exaggerated colours, as in [[see:The Scream]].
An early example of [[see:expressionism]].
Post-WWII movement, term popularised in the 1940s, pushing [[from:expressionism]] towards spontaneous abstract action, as with [[see:Jackson Pollock]].
Iconic [[see:abstract expressionism]] artist known for drip paintings and splatters.
Another artist associated with [[see:abstract expressionism]].
Provocative movement born of WWI disgust; its name may be a childish noise, or French [[from?:dada]], hobby horse, found by flicking through a dictionary.
German founder of [[see:Dadaism]], filmed in 1917 shouting in a toothpaste-tube-like costume; said to have picked its name from a dictionary.
Satirical Swiss club, also a publication, where [[see:Dadaism]] was founded.
Said to have found the name of [[see:Dadaism]] in a French dictionary with [[see:Hugo Ball]].
[[see:Marcel Duchamp]]'s famous Dadaist work, simply a urinal, signed [[see:R. Mutt]].
Creator of [[see:Fountain]], with a female alter ego, [[see:Rrose Sélavy]].
Jess is surprised by Rob's British pronunciation; stress shifts depending on suffixes, as with [[see:urinary]] and [[see:urine]].
Compared with [[see:urinal]] to show stress shifting with what follows.
Rob claims nostalgia for an older pronunciation, while [[see:urinal]] keeps the stress pattern.
The name written on [[see:Fountain]], a pun on German [[see:Armut]], poverty.
[[see:Marcel Duchamp]]'s female alter ego, a pun on French [[see:Eros, c'est la vie]], sex is life.
Coined around 1917 by [[see:Guillaume Apollinaire]] for a movement beyond [[from:realism]], from French sur, above; it gave the adjective [[gave:surreal]].
A 1930s back-formation from [[from:surrealism]], so something surreal is like a surrealist's creation.
Movement rejecting idealisation in favour of ordinary life and social conditions, in art and literature; [[gave:surrealism]] meant going beyond it.
Coined [[see:surrealism]] for a movement beyond realism.
A fancy-sounding French technique name that just means gluing.
French for chewed paper.
French for cutouts.
Named after [[from:Étienne de Silhouette]], perhaps for cheap portraits matching his frugality, his brief term, or simply because he made silhouettes himself.
1700s French controller-general known for petty austerity, after whom [[see:silhouette]] is named.
From Latin [[from:miniare]], to paint red, from [[from:minium]]; first a manuscript illumination, it came to mean small through association with [[unrelated:minimum]] and [[unrelated:minuscule]].
Assumed short for [[from:miniature]], as in mini camera or miniskirt.
From a Latin root meaning small, unrelated to [[unrelated:miniature]].
From the Latin root meaning small, unlike [[unrelated:miniature]].
Shares the Latin small root with [[same-root:minor]], but is unrelated to [[unrelated:miniature]].
From the Latin root meaning small, unrelated to [[unrelated:miniature]].
A lead-based red paint used to illuminate medieval manuscripts, giving their red-orange colour and the word [[gave:miniature]].
Early paragraph marks usually painted in red-orange [[see:minium]].
16th-century small portraits given to loved ones, which fixed the small sense of [[see:miniature]]; [[see:Henry VIII]] married based on one; often done as [[see:silhouette]]s.
Married one of his wives on the strength of a [[see:portrait miniature]] and was upset when she arrived.
Same source as [[same-root:portray]]; literally to draw forth or trace out, from Latin [[from:trahere]], with nothing implying a person.
With portrayal, shares its source with [[same-root:portrait]].
Mona is a contraction of [[from:Madonna]], so my lady Lisa; only the English name for the painting, which is smaller than expected.
The Italian name of the [[equivalent:Mona Lisa]], punning on the sitter's name, [[see:Lisa del Giocondo]].
The sitter of the [[see:Mona Lisa]], whose surname is punned on in [[see:La Gioconda]].
From French crayon, originally chalk pencil and now just pencil, from Latin [[from:creta]], chalk.
Latin for chalk or pipe clay, of unclear origin: maybe earth from [[from?:Crete]], or a Celtic word for clay; gave [[gave:crayon]] and [[gave:Cretaceous]].
From [[from:creta]], chalk.
Like [[see:creta]], an unresolved question: was copper named after [[see:Cyprus]] or Cyprus after copper?
Romans got [[see:copper]] from there, but it is unknown which name came first.
Cypress trees have the same naming puzzle as [[see:copper]] and [[see:Cyprus]].
Pigment in heated beeswax, used in ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome; the grandparent of the modern [[see:crayon]].
Coined in 1903 by [[see:Alice Stead Binney]] from [[from:crayon]] and [[from:oleaginous]], oily, for the paraffin wax.
Coined the name [[see:Crayola]] in 1903.
Rarest Crayola, made 1997–1998 before becoming [[see:Scarlet]]; named for Paralympian [[see:Gary K. Woodring]], the torch being the Olympic torch.
The later name of [[see:Torch Red]].
Gold-medal Paralympian and prosthetics chief honoured by [[see:Torch Red]], named by one of his clients who won a contest.
Yellow-orange Crayola retired in 2017 for [[see:Bluetiful]], sparking a collecting frenzy; the first removed from the box, reintroduced in 2025.
Blue Crayola that replaced [[see:Dandelion]], inspired by the newly discovered [[see:YInMn Blue]].
Newly discovered pigment that inspired [[see:Bluetiful]].
From [[from:porphyra]], a pigment traded as a symbol of wealth and colour of royal robes.
Crayola colour shortened from [[from:Flesh Tint]] in 1949, briefly [[see:Pink Beige]], then renamed [[gave:Peach]] in 1962.
Crayola name from 1903 to 1949 for a white skin colour, later shortened to [[gave:Flesh]].
Briefly the name of the [[see:Flesh]] crayon for two years after 1956.
Name of the former [[from:Flesh]] crayon since 1962; the 24-box light orange until [[see:Apricot]] replaced it.
Replaced [[see:Peach]] in the 24-crayon box in the mid-1990s.
Crayola colour from 1949, renamed [[gave:Midnight Blue]] in 1958 because Prussia was no longer relevant.
The 1958 renaming of [[from:Prussian Blue]].
